title: The Palace of Eternal Youth
subtitle: In Heaven Let Us Be Two Birds Flying Together, on Earth Let Us Be Two Branches Intertwined
description: "The Palace of Eternal Youth" is a chuanqi play by the Qing-dynasty playwright Hong Sheng, based on Bai Juyi's "Song of Everlasting Regret," Chen Hong's "The Tale of the Song of Everlasting Regret," and Bai Pu's "Rain on the Plane Tree." In fifty scenes, it traces the love story of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang and Yang Guifei, interwoven with the cataclysmic An Lushan Rebellion—both a poignant love epic and a grand historical drama reflecting on the rise and fall of dynasties.

route.title: The Palace of Eternal Youth: This Everlasting Regret Will Never End
route.intro:
In heaven let us be two birds flying together, / On earth let us be two branches intertwined. / Heaven and earth may long endure, but they will come to an end; / This everlasting regret will never end.
Hong Sheng (1645–1704), a native of Qiantang, Zhejiang (present-day Hangzhou), was born into an official family and was a student at the Imperial Academy. He spent over a decade completing "The Palace of Eternal Youth," revising his manuscript three times. As soon as it appeared, it took the capital by storm—"Every household packed up and put away, every door spoke of nothing but 'Beware' " ('Beware' being the first line of the 'Lute Song' scene in the play). Yet fate played a cruel trick: because the play was performed during a period of national mourning, Hong Sheng was stripped of his status at the Imperial Academy, forced into obscurity, and eventually drowned in a drunken fall into the water at Wuzhen. "The Palace of Eternal Youth" is both the rainbow-hued robes and feathered garments of the Huaqing Pool and the handful of yellow earth beneath Mawei Slope. Let us enter the Tang dynasty's glorious capital Chang'an, and amid the hot springs of Lishan and the Dragon Pond of Xingqing Palace, look back upon that epic love story—of splendor pushed to its extreme, of life and death bound by promises, a love that has captivated the ages.

stops.title: Stop One: Imperial Bath at the Huaqing Palace on Lishan
stops.content: In the Kaiyuan and Tianbao reigns of the great Tang dynasty, the realm had known peace for a long time. Emperor Xuanzong, Li Longji, had been on the throne for thirty years, his civil and military achievements at their zenith. At a palace banquet, he saw the wife of Prince Shou, Yang Yuhuan—"One backward glance, a hundred smiles bloom; the painted ladies of the six palaces lose all their charm." He immediately had her ordained as a Daoist nun, given the style Taizhen, and then brought into the palace and installed as his Precious Consort. From then on, "the spring nights were too short, the sun rose too high; from then on, the sovereign held no early court." The Huaqing Palace Ruins at the northern foot of Mount Li are the most passionate witness to the love of Li and Yang. Emperor Xuanzong built for Yang Guifei the Lotus Flower Pool, the Crabapple Flower Pool, and other hot spring baths. Every year from the tenth month until the following spring, they spent their days here. "In the spring chill, she was granted a bath in the Huaqing Pool; the warm spring water, slippery and smooth, washed her alabaster skin"—Bai Juyi's poem froze that moment of tenderness into eternity. Strolling through the ruins, the remnants of the imperial baths are still warm, the millenary hot springs still bubble and flow—as if the Favored Grace's powder and fragrance have not yet fully faded.

stops.title: Stop Two: Vows at the Palace of Eternal Youth
stops.content: On the evening of Seventh-Day Night of the Tianbao reign, lamps swayed within the Palace of Eternal Youth, the Milky Way stretched across the sky. Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guifei stood shoulder to shoulder, gazing up at the stars of the Cowherd and the Weaving Maid, reflecting on how the heavenly lovers met only once a year while they themselves enjoyed daily companionship. They burned incense and pledged: "In heaven let us be two birds flying together, on earth let us be two branches intertwined"—no matter in heaven or on earth, life after life, they would never part. The Daming Palace Ruins, where the Palace of Eternal Youth stood, is the most magnificent palace complex of the Tang dynasty, covering 3.2 square kilometers. The foundations of Hanyuan Hall, Linde Hall, and other buildings still remain, giving a hint of their former splendor. Standing on the site and looking around—1,300 years ago, at dusk, Emperor Xuanzong composed the "Rainbow-Hued Feathered Robes Melody" here for Yang Guifei, teaching it to the Pear Garden musicians. The historical turning point—"The war drums from Yuyang shook the earth, shattering the strains of the Rainbow-Hued Feathered Robes air"—was about to unfold within these magnificent halls.

stops.title: Stop Three: Sudden Upheaval and the Burial of Jade
stops.content: In the eleventh month of the fourteenth year of the Tianbao reign (755 AD), An Lushan raised his rebel army in Fanyang. "The war drums from Yuyang shook the earth, shattering the strains of the Rainbow-Hued Feathered Robes air"—Hong Sheng used a masterful word "shattering" here: not "breaking," not "stopping," but "shattering," as if the drums were not coming from distant Youzhou but striking directly the surface of the warm Huaqing Pool, penetrating the swirling skirts of the Rainbow-Hued Feathered Robes. Luoyang fell quickly. The famed general Geshu Han was forced to defend the Tong Pass, but his 200,000-strong army was routed, leaving the capital Chang'an wide open. The seventy-two-year-old Li Longji, in panic, decided to flee westward. The emperor who had single-handedly created the Kaiyuan Golden Age now dared not even leave through the main gate. He slipped out through Yanqiu Gate, accompanied only by Yang Guifei and her sisters, a few princes, the eunuch Gao Lishi, and a small contingent of imperial guards. Just as Hong Sheng wrote in "The Palace of Eternal Youth—Sudden Upheaval": "Steadfast and serene the palace feasts and revels; tumultuous and turbulent the border rebels rise." When the imperial carriage reached Mawei Station (present-day Mawei Slope in Xingping, Shaanxi), tragedy struck. The army refused to advance; swords were drawn. The imperial guards first killed Chancellor Yang Guozhong, then surrounded the station, demanding that Xuanzong execute Yang Guifei. Historical records present the most heartbreaking scene: Gao Lishi led Yang Yuhuan into a Buddhist shrine; a white silk sash hung from a pear tree. On the fourteenth day of the sixth month of the fifteenth Tianbao year, at thirty-eight years old, Yang Yuhuan was strangled before the shrine. Bai Juyi wrote: "The sovereign covered his face, powerless to save her; turning back, tears and blood flowed together." The most exalted emperor, before his most beloved woman, was utterly powerless. In the "Burial of Jade" scene, Hong Sheng, through the voice of Chen Xuanli, articulated the cold logic: "Your subject advises Your Majesty: Though the Favored Grace is innocent, Yang Guozhong was indeed her elder brother. Now that he is by Your Majesty's side, the army's hearts are uneasy."—It was not your fault, nor hers; it was fate's fault. Looking back at Chang'an, that glorious capital once visited by envoys from a hundred nations, now lay under the iron heel of the rebels. The Daming Palace Ruins' Hanyuan Hall and Linde Hall—those carved beams, painted rafters, golden bricks and jade-green tiles—were reduced to rubble and ruin in the flames of the An Lushan Rebellion. This magnificent palace complex of 3.2 square kilometers bore witness to Li Longji's youthful ambition, his governing aspirations, and his ignominious flight. Standing on the vast rammed-earth platform of Hanyuan Hall, a sense of historical desolation washes over you—once, civil and military officials lined up on this very platform to pay homage to the Son of Heaven; once, envoys from a hundred nations entered through the Vermilion Phoenix Gate into the world's most magnificent palace. After the An Lushan Rebellion, all of this was gone. Go also to the Huaqing Palace Ruins—the hot spring waters of the Lotus Pool and Crabapple Pool still bubble and flow; the sunset over Mount Li still glows blood-red. But the Favored Grace whom "the maidservants helped rise, delicate and languid," and the emperor who "from then on held no early court" will never return. Beneath that handful of yellow earth at Mawei Slope lies buried not only a peerless beauty, but the final glory of the entire High Tang.

stops.title: Stop Four: Listening to the Bells at Jiange Pavilion in the Rainy Night
stops.content: After the An Lushan Rebellion was pacified, the former emperor, now retired, returned from Shu to Chang'an, passing through Jiange. This was the throat of the entry into Shu—sheer cliffs, suspended plank roads, "one man could hold the pass against ten thousand." Rain fell through the night; the mountain wind, laden with cold rain, blew through the window lattices of the post-house. Copper bells hung from the eaves clanged in the wind and rain—each chime striking his heart. He sat alone before a solitary lamp; the candle flame flickered, casting shadows over his white hair and empty sleeves. There was no one attending him; even Gao Lishi had been dismissed. At this moment, he wanted only to be alone, alone with thoughts of that wisp of fragrant soul beneath Mawei Slope. Hong Sheng wrote this scene with heartbreaking detail: the retired emperor, drowsy in the sound of rain, dreamed that Yang Guifei descended on a phoenix from heaven, and the two were reunited in the clouds. He was about to reach for her sleeve when a sudden burst of bell-ringing woke him. The post-house before him was as cold and desolate as ever; the rain outside was heavier, the bells beneath the eaves more urgent. Bai Juyi's poem here became the bleakest soliloquy on stage: "Fireflies flitted in the evening hall, their silent thoughts profound; the solitary lamp burned low, sleep still would not come. The slow bell and drum marked the first watch of the long night; the shimmering River of Stars heralded the approach of dawn." Under that solitary lamp sat not the once-exalted emperor who had galloped at Lishan and composed the Rainbow-Hued Feathered Robes, but an old man who had lost everything. Upon returning to the capital, he took up residence in Xingqing Palace. This had been his princely residence during the Kaiyuan reign, when he was Prince of Linzi—the most spirited years of his life. Xingqing Palace had the Dragon Pool with its shimmering waters, surrounded by peonies that bloomed in full glory every spring. He and Yang Guifei had once admired the peonies by the Aloeswood Pavilion; Li Bai stood nearby, improvising the immortal lines "Clouds call to mind her garments, flowers her face." Now, the people were gone, the halls empty. The Dragon Pool's waters still rippled blue; the peonies by the Aloeswood Pavilion still bloomed year after year—but the woman who had leaned in his arm admiring the flowers would never return. He ordered Yang Guifei's remains secretly reburied, only to find that "beneath the earth of Mawei Slope, there was no jade countenance, only an empty grave"—nothing remained but a fragrance pouch. He held that pouch, as if he could still smell the lingering warmth of the Favored Grace's body. In the "Lamenting the Portrait" scene, Hong Sheng, through Xuanzong's voice, expressed endless regret: "It was I who betrayed our deep vows, who failed your boundless love." Every dusk, he stood alone by the Dragon Pool. The pool reflected a setting sun and a white-haired old man. The Pear Garden musicians had long scattered—some dead in the war, others wandering the land. Occasionally he would have Gao Lishi find one or two old musicians to play half a tune—only half, because hearing the opening was enough to release tears he could no longer hold back. The site of Xingqing Palace lies east of today's Daming Palace Ruins. Though it no longer exists, standing on the site of Hanyuan Hall at the Daming Palace and gazing eastward, the sunset glow of 1,300 years ago is the same color as the one falling on your face today. Go again to the Huaqing Palace Ruins at the northern foot of Mount Li. Touch those stones steeped in hot spring waters for over a thousand years—they are warm still, but the woman with hair like clouds never again rose from the Crabapple Pool. The regret stretches on, endless, eternal.

stops.title: Stop Five: Reunion in the Moon Palace
stops.content: Here is "The Palace of Eternal Youth's" most moving invention. Hong Sheng did not stop, as Bai Juyi did, at "this everlasting regret will never end." Instead, he gave this tragic imperial couple a reunion beyond life and death. After Yang Guifei's death, her faithful spirit drifted to Penglai Immortal Mountain, where she was enshrined as the Perfected Being Taizhen. Meanwhile, Emperor Xuanzong pined for her in the mortal world day and night. He summoned the Daoist Yang Tongyou to search heaven and earth for the Favored Grace's soul. Finally, on the night of the full moon of the eighth month, an immortal bridge descended from heaven. Xuanzong ascended and was reunited with Yang Yuhuan in the Moon Palace. They grasped each other's hands, gazing through tear-filled eyes, ten thousand words condensed into a single sigh—through all tribulations, their true feelings remained unchanged. This ending embodies Hong Sheng's deepest compassion. He did not, as traditional historians did, blame the An Lushan Rebellion on a "woman's curse." Nor did he criticize the imperial love affair from a moralistic standpoint. He simply wrote the most elemental story: two people in love, who once possessed the most radiant years, experienced the most devastating separation, and ultimately achieved immortality in the realm of art. Today, standing before the Crabapple Pool at the Huaqing Palace Ruins, the hot spring mist swirls, the sunset over Mount Li glows red. Go to the Daming Palace Ruins and gaze into the distance from the foundations of Hanyuan Hall—the grass growing between the bricks, the clouds drifting across the sky, the faint silhouette of the Zhongnan Mountains in the distance—nothing has changed from what Li Longji saw 1,300 years ago. History has turned page after page, but only the moon over Mount Li still shines on that pair of old friends from the Song of Everlasting Regret.

stops.title: Stop Six: Remembering Eternal Youth from Chang'an's City Wall
stops.content:
The ruins of Huaqing Palace and Daming Palace face each other across the city of Chang'an. But if you want a single spot that takes in the entire story, nothing beats climbing the Xi'an City Wall. This ancient city wall, the largest and best-preserved in China, is 13.7 kilometers in circumference. Built during the Ming dynasty's Hongwu reign, it stands twelve meters high. Though it is not the original Tang dynasty Chang'an city wall—that once grandest of all capital walls has long been lost to history—the ground beneath your feet is still the soil of Tang Chang'an. Thirteen centuries ago, the splendor of envoys from a hundred nations unfolded on this very land. Li Longji created the Kaiyuan Golden Age here, and here he met the woman who would change his life.

You can cycle or stroll along the wall. When tired, rest in a watchtower and listen to the city-wall park below: elderly folks playing erhu and singing Qinqiang opera, their desolate, soaring tunes echoing off the walls—perhaps the last resonance of the great Tang's surviving melodies. In the distance, the Small Wild Goose Pagoda stands silently in the twilight. This Tang-dynasty, close-eaved brick pagoda has weathered over 1,300 years of wind and rain, standing together with the Xi'an City Wall as guardians of the city's deepest memories. The flames of the An Lushan Rebellion have long since dissipated; the love of Li Longji and Yang Yuhuan has long been transformed into the Song of Everlasting Regret in black ink on white paper. Yet every brick of the Xi'an City Wall still carries the warmth of that era.

At dusk, the setting sun casts the wall's shadow long, long. Standing on the gate tower of Yongning Gate and looking westward, Mount Li appears faintly on the horizon. At this very moment 1,300 years ago, that white-haired retired emperor might have been sitting alone by the Dragon Pool of Xingqing Palace, watching the same setting sun, thinking the same thoughts. The city wall is silent, but it quietly guards the memory of Chang'an, and that never-fading song: Heaven and earth may long endure, but they will come to an end; this everlasting regret will never end.
